blocks.content: Every algorithm covered in this module, First Come First Served, Shortest Job First, Priority Scheduling and Round Robin, was ultimately judged using the same small set of precisely defined metrics. It is not enough to have an intuitive sense that one schedule feels faster or fairer than another. Getting these formulas exactly right, not just approximately right, is what separates a candidate who can correctly trace through a scheduling problem under interview or exam pressure from one who cannot.

This closing chapter of the CPU Scheduling module collects every metric used throughout the module in one place, defines each one with its exact formula, and works through a single, fully worked numeric example that computes all of them together for three processes. It also clears up the single most common point of confusion in this entire area, the difference between waiting time and response time, and ends with a formula reference table built for quick review before an interview or exam.
1. Arrival Time and Burst Time: The Two Given Values
blocks.text: 1. Arrival Time and Burst Time: The Two Given Values

blocks.content: Two of the six metrics in this chapter are not calculated at all, they are simply given as input to a scheduling problem. Every other metric is derived from these two starting numbers, so it is worth being precise about what each one actually represents before building anything on top of them.
Arrival Time

Arrival time is the moment a process enters the ready queue, ready to be considered for the CPU. It is denoted AT and is always provided directly in a scheduling problem, never computed. A process with arrival time 3 simply means it becomes eligible to run starting at time 3, not a moment before.
Burst Time

Burst time is the total amount of CPU time a process needs to complete its work, denoted BT. Like arrival time, it is given, not calculated, and it represents the full amount of CPU execution required, regardless of how many separate turns on the CPU it takes to deliver that total. If a process is preempted partway through, the remaining burst time is simply whatever total is left to run.

blocks.title: Given, not derived
blocks.content: Arrival time and burst time are the only two values you receive as input to a scheduling problem. Every metric explained in the rest of this chapter, completion time, turnaround time, waiting time and response time, is calculated from these two numbers together with the schedule itself.
2. Completion Time, Turnaround Time and Waiting Time
blocks.text: 2. Completion Time, Turnaround Time and Waiting Time

blocks.content: These next three metrics build directly on each other, and each one is read off or calculated in a specific, exact way. Working through them in order, completion time first, then turnaround time, then waiting time, is the safest way to avoid mixing up the formulas.
Completion Time

Completion time, denoted CT, is the exact moment a process finishes executing. It does not come from a formula of its own, it is read directly off a Gantt chart, the point on the timeline where that process last unit of CPU execution ends. Every other metric in this section is built from this one observed value.
Turnaround Time

Turnaround time, denoted TAT, is the total time a process spends in the system, measured from the moment it arrives to the moment it finishes. The formula is Turnaround Time equals Completion Time minus Arrival Time, written TAT = CT minus AT. It captures the entire span of a process life, both the time it spent waiting and the time it spent actually running.
Waiting Time

Waiting time, denoted WT, is the portion of that total span spent sitting in the ready queue, not running. The formula is Waiting Time equals Turnaround Time minus Burst Time, written WT = TAT minus BT. Since turnaround time already accounts for the entire time in the system and burst time is the portion actually spent running, subtracting one from the other leaves exactly the time spent waiting.

Completion time is read off the chart. Turnaround time is completion time minus arrival time. Waiting time is turnaround time minus burst time. Each formula only makes sense once the one before it is correct.
3. Response Time

Response time, denoted RT, is the time from a process arrival until it first gets the CPU, and only the first time. The formula is Response Time equals First Start Time minus Arrival Time, written RT = First Start Time minus AT. This is the metric most often confused with waiting time, and the distinction gets its own full section later in this chapter.

blocks.title: Only the first turn counts
blocks.content: Response time freezes the instant a process is first given the CPU. Anything that happens afterward, including being preempted and forced to wait again, has no effect on response time at all. It is purely about how quickly a process gets its first chance to run.

In a non preemptive scheduler, where a process runs to completion the moment it starts, response time and waiting time always end up equal, since a process only ever waits once, before that single uninterrupted run. Under a preemptive scheduler that equality no longer holds, which is exactly what the worked example later in this chapter demonstrates.
4. A Fully Worked Example: Every Metric Together
blocks.text: 4. A Fully Worked Example: Every Metric Together

blocks.content: Numbers make all four formulas concrete at once. Take three processes, P1, P2 and P3, with the arrival and burst times given below, and trace them through a simple first come first served style schedule.

P1 arrives at time 0 and, being the only process ready, starts immediately and runs for its full burst of 4 units, finishing at time 4. P2 arrived earlier, at time 1, but had to wait for the CPU, so it starts at time 4 and runs for 3 units, finishing at time 7. P3 does not arrive until time 8, so once P2 finishes at time 7 the CPU has nothing to do and sits idle for one unit, from 7 to 8, until P3 finally shows up and runs for its full burst of 5 units, finishing at time 13.

P2 runs from 4 to 7   (burst 3, arrived at time 1, waited from 1 until start at 4)
CPU sits idle from 7 to 8, because P3 has not arrived yet
P3 runs from 8 to 13  (burst 5, arrived at time 8, starts immediately since the CPU is idle)

blocks.content: With completion time read directly off this chart, every other metric follows from the formulas already defined. The table below computes all six metrics, the two given values, arrival time and burst time, together with completion time, turnaround time, waiting time and response time, side by side for all three processes.

Notice that for every process here, waiting time and response time come out identical, P1 shows 0 and 0, P2 shows 3 and 3, P3 shows 0 and 0. That is not a coincidence, it is a direct consequence of using a non preemptive schedule, where each process waits exactly once, before its single uninterrupted run, so its first and only wait is also its entire wait. Section 6 of this chapter walks through a small preemptive example where this stops being true.
5. System Level Metrics

The four metrics covered so far, completion time, turnaround time, waiting time and response time, are all per process, each one describes a single process experience. Scheduling algorithms are also judged by system level metrics that describe how the CPU and the whole batch of processes performed together.
CPU Utilization

CPU Utilization measures the percentage of time the CPU was actually busy doing useful work, as opposed to sitting idle waiting for a process to arrive. The formula is CPU Utilization equals Busy Time divided by Total Time. In the worked example above, the CPU was busy for 4 plus 3 plus 5, which is 12 units, out of a total elapsed time of 13 units, from time 0 to time 13, since the CPU sat idle for exactly 1 unit between P2 finishing and P3 arriving. That gives a CPU Utilization of 12 divided by 13, which is about 92.3 percent.
Throughput

Throughput measures the number of processes completed per unit of time. The formula is Throughput equals Number Of Processes Completed divided by Total Time. In the worked example, all three processes completed within 13 time units, giving a throughput of 3 divided by 13, or about 0.23 processes per unit of time, roughly one process finishing every 4 to 5 time units.
Average Waiting Time and Average Turnaround Time
blocks.text: Average Waiting Time and Average Turnaround Time

blocks.content: These two are simply the mean of the per process values already computed, added together and divided by the number of processes. Using the same three process example, Average Waiting Time equals the sum of 0, 3 and 0, divided by 3, which is 1 unit. Average Turnaround Time equals the sum of 4, 6 and 5, divided by 3, which is 5 units. These averages, not any single process individual numbers, are what gets compared when judging one scheduling algorithm against another.
6. Response Time vs Waiting Time: Why They Get Confused
blocks.text: 6. Response Time vs Waiting Time: Why They Get Confused

blocks.content: Response time and waiting time are two of the most frequently confused metrics in this entire module, and the confusion is understandable, both describe time a process spends not running. The difference is what portion of that time each one is counting.

["Waiting time accumulates across the entire time a process spends in the ready queue, including every separate wait if the process is preempted more than once.","Response time only ever measures the gap between arrival and the very first time the process gets the CPU. Anything that happens after that first run, including further waits, has no effect on it.","A process can therefore have a short response time and still end up with a long total waiting time, if it gets preempted repeatedly after that fast first start."]
items: Waiting time accumulates across the entire time a process spends in the ready queue, including every separate wait if the process is preempted more than once.
Response time only ever measures the gap between arrival and the very first time the process gets the CPU. Anything that happens after that first run, including further waits, has no effect on it.
A process can therefore have a short response time and still end up with a long total waiting time, if it gets preempted repeatedly after that fast first start.

blocks.content: A small preemptive example makes this concrete. Suppose process X arrives at time 0 with a total burst of 6 units. It gets the CPU immediately and runs from time 0 to time 2, then gets preempted, 2 units into its 6 unit burst, with 4 units still remaining. Process Y then arrives and runs from time 2 to time 5. Once Y finishes, X resumes and runs its remaining 4 units, from time 5 to time 9, finally completing.
{"headers":["Process","First Starts At","Preempted At","Resumes At","Finishes At"],"rows":[["X","0","2","5","9"]]}

Process X has a response time of 0, since it got the CPU the instant it arrived at time 0. Its turnaround time is completion time minus arrival time, 9 minus 0, which is 9. Its waiting time is turnaround time minus burst time, 9 minus 6, which is 3, all of it accumulated during the single stretch from time 2 to time 5 while Y was running. X therefore shows an excellent response time of 0 alongside a real, nonzero waiting time of 3, precisely because it was preempted once after that fast first start.

Response time answers one question only, how quickly did this process first get the CPU. Waiting time answers a broader question, how much total time did this process spend not running, across every wait it ever had.

8. Common Mistakes
Confusing turnaround time with waiting time
blocks.text: Confusing turnaround time with waiting time

blocks.content: This is the single most frequent error in this entire topic. Turnaround time measures the whole time a process spends in the system, from arrival to finish, including the time it spent actually running. Waiting time measures only the portion spent waiting, with the burst time subtracted out. Reporting turnaround time when a question asks for waiting time, or the reverse, is an easy mistake that changes every number in an answer.
Treating response time as total wait
blocks.text: Treating response time as total wait

blocks.content: Response time is about the first CPU access only. It is tempting to treat it as a synonym for waiting time, but under any preemptive algorithm the two can diverge sharply, exactly as the worked example in the previous section shows, a process can have a response time of 0 and still accumulate real waiting time afterward.
Averaging incorrectly

Average waiting time and average turnaround time are simple means, the sum of the per process values divided by the number of processes, nothing more. The two mistakes that show up most often are summing the wrong column, mixing waiting time values into what should be a turnaround time average, and dividing by the wrong count, forgetting to include every process or accidentally including a process twice.
9. Closing: The Metrics Behind Every Algorithm in This Module
blocks.text: 9. Closing: The Metrics Behind Every Algorithm in This Module

blocks.content: Every sibling topic in the CPU Scheduling module, First Come First Served, Shortest Job First and its preemptive form Shortest Remaining Time First, Priority Scheduling, and Round Robin, uses exactly these metrics to judge and compare performance. None of those chapters introduces a different way of measuring how well an algorithm performed, they all reduce to the same six per process formulas and the same handful of system level averages defined in this chapter.

blocks.title: Quick recap to keep ready
blocks.content: Turnaround time is completion time minus arrival time. Waiting time is turnaround time minus burst time. Response time is the first start time minus arrival time, and only the first. CPU Utilization is busy time divided by total time. Throughput is processes completed divided by total time. Averages are simply the mean of the per process values across all processes.

With this formula toolkit fixed firmly in place, tracing through any scheduling problem in this module, no matter which algorithm is being asked about, comes down to the same reliable process, build the Gantt chart correctly first, then apply these exact formulas in order, completion time, then turnaround time, then waiting time, then response time, one process at a time.
